retrieval_text: A 4-year-old boy presented with bilateral cataracts and poor vision. His parents noted that his physical and mental development was typical until he was 2 years old. After that age, he began experiencing difficulties in learning and communicating. Additionally, oculo-digital sign and self-injury behaviors were observed.

The patient is a 23-year-old female, height 165 cm, weight 36 kg. She exhibited developmental delay at the age of three and cognitive impairment that became noticeable during elementary school, leading to her enrollment in a special school for 12 years with below-average academic performance. At the age of 12, she experienced gait disturbance due to weakness in the right lower extremities.

A 14-month-old male of Asian and Caucasian descent presented with an 8-month history of recurrent cough, rapid breathing, and low blood oxygen levels, necessitating multiple hospital admissions. He was born full-term with an uncomplicated neonatal period and was of average size for gestational age. Early infancy was notable only for mild eczema, and he received all routine vaccinations. Family history was negative for significant medical or genetic conditions. He lived with both parents and was not on any medications. At 6 months of age, he presented with a 2-week history of dry cough and low oxygen levels, as detected by a home monitoring device (SpO2: 83–91%) at night. Physical examination revealed rapid breathing, subcostal retractions, decreased breath sounds, mild scattered wheezes, and bilateral crackles, without fever.

A 21-year-old male presented with pain and recurrent nodular swelling over the right foot for the past four years. He works as a farmer. Two years after the onset of painful swellings, there was a history of a sinus from the foot discharging pus with dark-colored granules. The patient had close contact with an active case of pulmonary tuberculosis (his wife). Following the onset of the discharge, the patient visited a local practitioner who sent the pus for culture and sensitivity testing. The patient was started on oral antibiotics based on the sensitivity results. The discharge mildly decreased with oral antibiotics but persisted, and the patient was advised to use local dressings. Due to the persistent discharging sinus, the patient eventually presented to the outpatient department of our hospital. On local examination, multiple nodular swellings were observed over the dorsum, medial, and lateral aspects of the midfoot. There was a discharging sinus over the dorsum of the midfoot, adherent to the bone, with non-undermined margins. There was diffuse tenderness in the mid and forefoot, and movements in these areas were painful and restricted.

An 82-year-old man reported experiencing blurred vision and a pressure-like sensation in the left eye for the past year. His medical history included hypertension, glaucoma, and prostate cancer. Visual acuity, corrected to the best possible level, was 20/20 in both eyes. He successfully identified all Ishihara plates with both eyes. Pupil size was 3 mm bilaterally. A grade one relative afferent pupillary defect was noted in the left eye. Examination of the left optic disc revealed mild elevation and indistinct nasal margins, with unobscured blood vessels and no hemorrhages or exudates. Subtle macular edema, a few choroidal folds, and tortuous retinal vessels were observed in the left eye. The right optic disc appeared normal. The remainder of the neuro-ophthalmic examination was unremarkable, with no skin lesions indicative of neurofibromatosis.

A 42-year-old Japanese woman, who has had one pregnancy and one normal vaginal delivery 13 years ago, showed an increase in uterine size during a screening. She reported recent lower abdominal pain and had been experiencing urinary incontinence and constipation for several months. During a pelvic examination, a fist-sized lump was noted in the uterus and left ovary. The vulva and vagina appeared normal. The portio was not clearly visible, making endometrial smear tests and uteroscopy unfeasible.

A 62-year-old male visited the dermatology clinic with multiple discharging sinuses located on the neck and right axillary region, persisting for 2 months. The patient reported a gradual increase in the lesion size with minimal discharge. He denied any history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or tuberculosis. The patient mentioned that he is a retired teacher residing in California for the past decade and travels to India annually. Physical examination revealed multiple discharging sinuses on the anterior neck and right axilla, with mild erythema around the sinus openings and minimal serosanguinous discharge. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities.

A 10-month-old girl was brought to the ophthalmic emergency room at King Abdulaziz University Hospital, Riyadh, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, due to vitreous hemorrhage in the right eye. Her parents had observed an outward deviation of her right eye for the past 5 weeks. They reported no history of ocular or head trauma and no systemic disease. Ophthalmic examination revealed a right exotropia measuring 30 prism diopters. The vision in the right eye was central, steady, and unmaintained, and she resisted occlusion of the left eye. Extra-ocular muscle movements were full.

A four-year-old boy was referred to the Division of Pediatric Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute, Baltimore, Maryland for bilateral partial lens dislocation. Two months earlier, the patient had failed a vision screening at school and was referred for further evaluation. The child did not report any visual symptoms; however, the family observed that he would sit very close to the television and focus closely on toys. He had no history of trauma, developmental issues, or hearing deficits. Genetic screening at birth was normal. The family history was negative for ocular problems other than myopia in his mother.

A 38-year-old male was admitted to the Neurology Department at the Hillel Yaffe Medical Center with a severe headache lasting two days, accompanied by dizziness and confusion. Physical and neurological examinations were unremarkable.

A 47-year-old male presented to the emergency department with complaints of blurred vision and pain in his left eye for the past four weeks. Initially, the patient attributed these symptoms to a headache or a previous condition related to his medical history of multiple sclerosis. Over time, his vision worsened, accompanied by the appearance of floaters and increased pain two weeks before seeking medical attention.
A 15-year-old female presented with pain on the left side of the abdomen and extended menstrual bleeding.

A three-year-old girl presented with severe abdominal pain, food refusal, constipation, and fever over the past seven days. She was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with non-consanguineous parents, and had a birth weight of 3130 g. Clinical examination revealed telecanthus, a prominent nasal bridge, a short philtrum, small hands, an anteriorized anus, severe psychomotor delay, absence of expressive language, and dysphagia. The main symptoms included persistent, inconsolable crying, abdominal distension, and mild fever.
A 47-year-old male experienced hematochezia following a gastrointestinal infection.

A 57-year-old Caucasian male presented with acute pneumonia and progressive difficulty swallowing. He reported painless swallowing difficulties, dry mouth, hoarseness, and a sensation of a mass in the upper esophagus. His medical history includes type II diabetes, chronic bronchitis, chronic gastritis, urate nephropathy with a history of kidney stones, and coronary artery disease. The patient has a history of daily alcohol and nicotine use for 40 years. Physical examination revealed bilateral eyelid drooping and mild facial weakness.
A 61-year-old Chinese male with a history of grade 1 hypertension reported experiencing right lower abdominal distention and intermittent upper abdominal pain for a duration of 4 months.

Mr. MT, a 32-year-old male, has been married for 11 years and has 5 children. He has no history of somatic or psychiatric conditions. He completed secondary school and works as a builder. He has no history of substance use except for smoking, which he quit 4 years ago. The patient was referred for psychiatric examination after consultations with urologists, neurologists, and general practitioners. A few minutes (10–15 minutes) after each ejaculation, he experiences intense fatigue, severe muscle, bone, and joint pain lasting 3–7 days. He also reports sneezing, eye redness, itching sensations throughout the body, and significant concentration difficulties. Additionally, he experiences temporary dental pain that resolves spontaneously. These symptoms occur with all forms of ejaculation, including nocturnal emission, masturbation, and vaginal ejaculation. The symptoms began at puberty (age 14) and have increased in severity and duration over time, initially lasting 3 days and now extending to 7 days, causing financial difficulties due to missed work. This has led to sexual avoidance behavior despite preserved sexual desire and normal erections. The frequency of sexual intercourse has decreased from twice a week to once a month. For the past 2 years, he has also experienced secondary premature ejaculation. On examination, the patient was in good general health, well-built, and had complete secondary sexual characteristics. His weight was 97 kg, height 180 cm, and blood pressure 120/80 mm/Hg. Clinical examinations, including neurological and urological assessments, were normal.
A 50-year-old male presented with difficulty swallowing and a progressively enlarging, painless swelling in the left submandibular region over a period of 4 months.

A 28-year-old male of mixed race has experienced scalp skin redundancy for two years. The condition is characterized by deep cerebriform folds and wrinkles, specifically in the parietal and occipital regions. The patient reports no comorbidities, no similar family history, no consanguinity, and no use of anabolic steroid drugs. Additionally, there is no history of skin or scalp inflammatory diseases. Neurological and ophthalmological examinations revealed no abnormalities.

A 4-year-old girl presented with blue sclera and wrinkled skin. She was the only child of parents who were third-degree relatives (father aged 30 years, mother aged 24 years). She was delivered at term via LSCS with a birth weight of 2.25 kg. The perinatal period was uneventful. She exhibited motor developmental delay and mild learning difficulty. Physical examination revealed a weight of 12 kg (<3rd percentile), height of 97 cm (3rd-10th percentile), and head circumference of 44 cm (<3rd percentile). Notable features included palpebral down slant, bilateral epicanthal folds, blue sclera, flat nasal bridge, sagging cheeks, and prominent ears. She had generalized loose, wrinkled skin folds, especially on the face, neck, abdomen, and extremities. Systemic examinations were normal. Skeletal evaluation indicated bilateral hip dislocation. Ophthalmologic examination confirmed blue sclera and shallow anterior chambers.
